countries.name: Angola
countries.ge_status: De facto GMO ban since a 2004 decree (food-aid imports allowed conditionally). No biosafety law, so no gene-editing policy. Restrictive.

countries.name: Burkina Faso
countries.ge_status: Commercialised Bt cotton (suspended ~2016 over fibre quality, not safety). Pro-biotech. 2023 ANB technical guide exempts genome-edited products with no foreign genes from the 2012 Biosafety Law (SDN-1 friendly).

countries.name: Cameroon
countries.ge_status: GM cotton field trials only (Sodecoton, 2012/2015); no commercial GM crop yet. New Biosafety Law No. 2025/6 (Apr 2025) modernised the framework.

countries.name: Côte d'Ivoire
countries.ge_status: No commercial GM crops or field trials. Operates under Biosafety Law No. 2016-553 (National Biosafety & Biosecurity Commission). Cautious, gradually engaging.

countries.name: Eswatini
countries.ge_status: Commercial Bt (GM) cotton. Biosafety Act 2012 explicitly covers emerging technologies incl. genome editing (regulated; no SDN-1 carve-out). Pro-biotech.

countries.name: Ethiopia
countries.ge_status: Bt cotton commercial; Bt maize approved for commercial production (2025). Published a Guideline on the Regulation of Genome-Edited Products (2024/25) with a risk-proportionate, case-by-case pathway. Meets 'already approved' on both counts.

countries.name: Ghana
countries.ge_status: PBR/Bt cowpea released for commercial use (NBA, Jul 2024). NBA approved genome editing of rice (Jul 2024). Pro-biotech; anti-GMO court suit dismissed May 2024.

countries.name: Guinea
countries.ge_status: No commercial GE crops; little/no documented national biosafety law. Activity is essentially nil.

countries.name: Guinea-Bissau
countries.ge_status: No commercial GM crops; (non-GM) cashew-dominated economy. Has a national biosafety law on paper; no domestic biotech programme.

countries.name: Kenya
countries.ge_status: Bt cotton commercial; 3 Bt maize varieties approved for commercialisation (Jan 2025); 2012 import ban lifted 2022. NBA Genome Editing Guidelines (rev. 2025) treat SDN-1/SDN-2 (no foreign DNA) as non-GMO case-by-case. Regional leader.

countries.name: Lesotho
countries.ge_status: Prohibits both cultivation and import of GMOs. No genome-editing guidelines. Restrictive.

countries.name: Madagascar
countries.ge_status: No commercial GM crops or documented field trials. Party to the Cartagena Protocol but no robust domestic biosafety framework. Cautious/undeveloped.

countries.name: Malawi
countries.ge_status: Bt cotton commercialised. Published Genome Editing Guidelines (Aug 2022) - among the first African nations - exempting SDN-1/non-novel-DNA edits from GMO regulation. Pro-biotech.

countries.name: Mozambique
countries.ge_status: TELA/Bt maize received provisional approval after confined trials; commercial release targeted from ~late 2024. Gene-editing guidelines drafted, awaiting validation. Pro-biotech.

countries.name: Nigeria
countries.ge_status: Commercial Bt cowpea (2019), TELA maize (2024, first GM cereal commercialised in Africa), Bt cotton. First African nation with science-based gene-editing guidelines (NBMA, 2020/22): SDN-1 edits exempt from GMO rules.

countries.name: Rwanda
countries.ge_status: No commercial GM crop yet (CBSD-resistant GM cassava in trials). Biosafety law promulgated Feb 2024; no GE-specific SDN-1 guidelines published yet. 'Already approved' overstates it.

countries.name: Senegal
countries.ge_status: No commercial GM crops; 2009 Biosafety Law (revised draft). No published GE guidelines yet but actively engaged - hosted an international genome-editing-in-crops workshop (Nov 2025).

countries.name: Sierra Leone
countries.ge_status: No commercial GM crops or trials. National Biosafety & Biosecurity Policy/Guidelines 2022 exist (loosely via EPA-SL). Minimal activity, capacity-constrained.

countries.name: South Africa
countries.ge_status: Africa's most advanced GM grower (maize, soy, cotton at scale). BUT in 2024 it upheld a 2021 decision to regulate ALL new breeding techniques (CRISPR/SDN editing) AS GMOs under the GMO Act 1997 - no SDN-1 exemption. For gene editing specifically it is among the world's most restrictive (EU/NZ/Peru-s

countries.name: Tanzania
countries.ge_status: No commercial GM crops; GMO maize field trials suspended in 2021 and none currently running. 2009 Biosafety Regulations impose strict liability that functions as a de facto ban. Classed as a regional resister. 'Mid adopter' is too optimistic.

countries.name: Uganda
countries.ge_status: No commercial GM crops despite extensive confined field trials (banana, cassava, maize). KEY: President Museveni has refused to sign the biosafety law twice; it remains in abeyance as of 2024/25 - so there is no legal commercial pathway. 'Fast follower' is optimistic.

countries.name: Zambia
countries.ge_status: No commercial GM cultivation; historically a resister (rejected GM food aid 2002). GM import ban lifted 2019; Biosafety Act 2007 + functioning National Biosafety Authority. GE guidelines only under development (experts convened May 2024). Still skeptical.

countries.name: Zimbabwe
countries.ge_status: GM cultivation prohibited (GM maize imports allowed only if milled). Classed as a resister, BUT the National Biotechnology Authority + AUDA-NEPAD ran 2024 workshops and Zimbabwe is listed (with Mozambique) as having drafted GE guidelines awaiting validation.

countries.name: Egypt
countries.ge_status: Approved Bt cotton historically but suspended GM planting in 2012; no current commercial GM. Notably permissive legal posture (no restriction on researching/producing/marketing GM) but a biosafety law drafted in 2011 never passed Parliament. Strong CRISPR (wheat) research base.

countries.name: Iran
countries.ge_status: GM (Bt) rice approved/released 2004 but cultivation halted 2005-06 and never resumed; some GM food imports allowed with labelling. 2009 Biosafety Law covers living GMOs only; no GE/SDN framework. Strong CRISPR research (AREEO) but governance instability.

countries.name: Iraq
countries.ge_status: No commercial GM crops; weak/undeveloped biosafety regime, no functional GMO approval system. No gene-editing framework. Institutional capacity weakened by years of conflict.

countries.name: Mauritania
countries.ge_status: No commercial GM crops or trials. President signed a national Biosafety Law in Aug 2022 (National Biosafety Authority, 150-day dossier review) - a framework exists on paper but is untested. Precautionary; essentially no biotech R&D.

countries.name: Morocco
countries.ge_status: No GM cultivation; precautionary. Published a National Biosafety Framework (2013) but never enacted a biosafety law - major gap. Ministry guidance justifies banning GE products from local cultivation/consumption. No genome-editing guidelines.

countries.name: Syria
countries.ge_status: No commercial GM crops. Party to Cartagena Protocol (2004); restrictive by default. Biosafety framework implementation stalled by lack of resources and prolonged conflict.

countries.name: Turkey
countries.ge_status: Cultivation BANNED. Biosafety Law No. 5977 (2010) bans GE plant/animal cultivation and GE seed planting; imports allowed only for animal feed, event-by-event (~36 corn/soy events); zero events for food or cultivation. No NGT carve-out.

countries.name: Argentina
countries.ge_status: One of the world's largest GM growers (soy, maize, cotton, HB4 drought-tolerant wheat). World's first NBT framework - Resolution 173/2015: SDN-1/edits with no transgene = non-GMO. The regional model.

countries.name: Belize
countries.ge_status: No commercial GM cultivation. Among Caribbean countries still developing a baseline biosafety bill - a basic GMO framework isn't even finalised. Cautious/undeveloped, CARICOM-aligned.

countries.name: Bolivia
countries.ge_status: ~10th-largest GM grower (~1.4M ha GM soybean). Oct 2024 approved a new GM soybean (restricted to biofuel use). No gene-editing framework; 2012 'Mother Earth Law' bans GMOs in centres of origin. Politically conflicted (agribusiness vs. central govt/indigenous networks).

countries.name: Brazil
countries.ge_status: 2nd-largest GM grower (soy, maize, cotton, beans). CTNBio Normative Resolution 16 (2018): SDN-1/SDN-2 without foreign DNA = conventional. Many products cleared (incl. 2026 gene-edited eucalyptus; 2025 gene-edited tilapia). Strongly pro-biotech.

countries.name: Dominican Republic
countries.ge_status: No commercial GM cultivation. Has a biosafety law (No. 219-15); MIMARENA is competent authority, CONABIO advises. No Argentina-style SDN-1 exemption yet; case-by-case under the Cartagena Protocol.

countries.name: Ecuador
countries.ge_status: Constitution (Art. 401, 2008) declares Ecuador a 'transgenic-free territory' - bans commercial GM cultivation. BUT a precision-breeding technical guide lets edits without foreign DNA register/market as conventional, so gene editing has a pathway despite the transgenic ban. Pragmatically opening (ban

countries.name: El Salvador
countries.ge_status: No GM crop approved for cultivation domestically. Signed the 2019 tri-national agreement (with Honduras/Guatemala): gene-edited crops not meeting the transgenic definition regulated as conventional. Framework largely on paper; implementation lags Honduras/Guatemala.

countries.name: Guatemala
countries.ge_status: Acuerdo Ministerial No. 271 (2019) already exempts plants with no added/novel-combination DNA from GMO regulation (part of the 2019 tri-national agreement). So a gene-editing pathway exists today - SDN-1 maize can be treated as conventional. The bottleneck is institutional capacity/political will, n

countries.name: Honduras
countries.ge_status: Only Central American country with commercial GM cultivation (GM maize since 2002; ~7 events; also GM rice). First in Central America to regulate NBTs - SENASA's 2019 technical regulation gives a simplified pathway; edits without foreign DNA = conventional.

countries.name: Mexico
countries.ge_status: GM corn cultivation not permitted; a 2023 presidential decree restricted GM corn. KEY UPDATE: after losing a USMCA dispute panel (Dec 2024), Mexico published cancellation of the GM-corn restrictions in Feb 2025, effectively lifting import limits. But domestic gene-editing/GM crop approval remains ve
countries.tier_note: Late to never (domestic cultivation; imports thawing)

countries.name: Nicaragua
countries.ge_status: No notable commercial GM cultivation. Cartagena Protocol LMO definition incorporated into domestic law; no Argentina-style exemption. Cautious; not part of the HN/GT/SV harmonisation bloc.

countries.name: Paraguay
countries.ge_status: World's ~4th soybean exporter; ~94% of soy, 36% maize, 56% cotton are GM. Adopted an SDN-1 exemption (2019, harmonised with Argentina/Brazil); CONBIO/SENAVE treat edits without foreign DNA as conventional. Pro-biotech.

countries.name: Peru
countries.ge_status: GM crop cultivation/import under a moratorium extended to 2035 (Law 31111). BUT in Mar 2026 the Ministry of Environment issued gene-editing guidelines (Min. Resolution D000068-2026-MINAM-DM) creating a process to assess whether edited products fall under the 'living modified organism' definition - e

countries.name: Suriname
countries.ge_status: No commercial GM cultivation. Among Caribbean countries still developing baseline biosafety legislation. Cautious/undeveloped; very small ag-biotech footprint.

countries.name: Venezuela
countries.ge_status: GM crops banned. Dec 2015 Seed Law prohibits production, import, commercialisation, release and use of transgenic seed (and bans plant-breeders' rights). Among the most anti-GMO globally; economic/institutional collapse further limits any framework. 'Late adopter' understates the barriers.

countries.name: Afghanistan
countries.ge_status: No commercial GM crops; no functional biosafety law or regulatory body. Effectively no policy; institutions severely constrained, especially post-2021.

countries.name: Bangladesh
countries.ge_status: Bt brinjal approved 2013, cultivated since 2014 (first GE food crop commercialised in a developing country). Ministry of Agriculture published SOPs for SDN-1/SDN-2 genome-edited plants (Dec 2023): edits free of exogenous DNA treated like conventional varieties. Among the most progressive in South As

countries.name: India
countries.ge_status: Bt cotton since 2002; GM mustard approved for environmental release 2022 (litigated). Mar 2022 Office Memorandum exempted SDN-1/SDN-2 plants free of exogenous DNA from EPA Rules; 2022 GE safety guidelines notified. In May/June 2025 ICAR released two genome-edited rice varieties (India's first GE cro

countries.name: Nepal
countries.ge_status: No commercial GM crops. National Biosafety Framework (2006) and Biotechnology Policy exist but are not effectively implemented (lacks enabling acts/regulations). Cautious but not hostile; main barrier is weak implementation capacity.

countries.name: Pakistan
countries.ge_status: Major Bt cotton grower since ~2010. Oct 2025 the National Biosafety Committee approved Pakistan's first GM sugarcane and new GM cotton varieties, plus 43 GM canola events for import. Under Biosafety Rules 2005, edits with no foreign gene fall outside GMO rules (de facto SDN-1 exemption); Cabinet app

countries.name: Sri Lanka
countries.ge_status: No GM cultivation; does not allow import of GE food/crops/animals. Only lab-level GE research. Restrictive/precautionary (reinforced by the 2021 organic-agriculture push). National Biosafety Act long delayed.

countries.name: Cambodia
countries.ge_status: No commercial GM crops; no functioning biosafety framework. Effectively no developed national biotech policy; reliant on regional ASEAN efforts.

countries.name: Indonesia
countries.ge_status: Commercial GM crops grown (corn, potato, sugarcane approved since ~2021). Drafted CRISPR/gene-editing regulation (2021); BPOM Regulation No. 19/2024 classifies genome-edited food case-by-case as GM or non-GM. Has both a GE framework AND approved GM crops.

countries.name: Lao PDR
countries.ge_status: No commercial GM crops; plant breeding is small, public-sector, donor-dependent. No agricultural gene-editing framework (a 2024 regulation covers medical biopharma/gene therapy only). Negligible biotech capacity.

countries.name: Malaysia
countries.ge_status: Biosafety Act 2007 regulates LMOs; no commercial GM crop cultivation; plant biotech development minimal. No gene-editing-specific framework / SDN-1 carve-out yet. Cautiously supportive in policy but little product development.

countries.name: Myanmar
countries.ge_status: Only Bt cotton approved; no other GM crops. National Biosafety Framework/Guidelines drafted but stuck pending ministerial approval since before the 2021 coup; no biosafety law passed. No GE framework.

countries.name: Philippines
countries.ge_status: One of Asia's most GM-permissive countries (Bt corn cultivation; imports). DA Memorandum Circular No. 8 (2022): edits without a novel combination of genetic material are conventional, not GMO (non-browning banana cleared 2023). BUT an April 2024 Court of Appeals writ of kalikasan halted Golden Rice

countries.name: Thailand
countries.ge_status: Historically banned GM crop cultivation. BUT in Jul 2024 the Ministry of Agriculture published genome-editing certification rules exempting SDN-1 (non-foreign-DNA) edits from GMO classification - making Thailand ~the 25th country to formally approve gene-edited crops. Anti-transgenic but newly pro-e

countries.name: Timor-Leste
countries.ge_status: No evidence of commercial GM crops or a functioning biosafety framework; not covered in regional regulatory trackers. Subsistence agriculture; minimal institutional capacity.

countries.name: Vietnam
countries.ge_status: Commercial GM maize cultivation since 2015. BREAKTHROUGH: the amended Law on Biodiversity (Law 146/2025/QH15) excludes gene-edited organisms lacking foreign DNA from GMO requirements via a self-determination notification to MARD. A concrete 2024-25 development beyond a mere 'fast follower' posture.

countries.name: China
countries.ge_status: GM cotton/papaya long-grown; Dec 2023 MARA approved GM corn and soybean (first GM staple crops), with further variety registration in 2024. MARA's Jan 2022 'Guidelines for Safety Evaluation of Gene-Edited Plants' give a streamlined pathway; Dec 2024 MARA issued 5 gene-edited event certificates for c

countries.name: Mongolia
countries.ge_status: No commercial GM crops; LMO provisions folded into Food/Food-Safety laws (2012) requiring registration and labelling - a precautionary regime, not a cultivation framework. No GE-specific framework. Pastoral economy = low demand for GM/GE crops.

countries.name: Albania
countries.ge_status: No commercial GM cultivation; EU-harmonised food law, restrictive in practice but not ideologically anti-GMO. Active EU accession candidate (negotiations opened 2024-25) - will inherit the EU's New Genomic Techniques (NGT) regulation (Council adopted Apr 2026; most provisions apply ~2028), under whi

countries.name: Azerbaijan
countries.ge_status: Bans GM cultivation; bans import/distribution of GM plants; GMOs prohibited in food production, with criminal liability for GMO use. Among the most restrictive; not on an EU or EAEU liberalising pathway.

countries.name: Belarus
countries.ge_status: No commercial GM cultivation, but the region's most developed biosafety/biotech R&D infrastructure (2006 genetic-engineering law; trial releases permitted; national biotech programme). No GE-specific exemption; EAEU/Russia-aligned, not EU.

countries.name: Bosnia & Herzegovina
countries.ge_status: Law on GMOs (2009); cultivation banned; import of EU-approved products permitted (GE soybean meal for feed). Explicitly harmonising with EU. EU candidate (status Dec 2022) but accession is distant, so will eventually inherit NGT rules - later than the active candidates.

countries.name: Kazakhstan
countries.ge_status: GE law (Art. 13) prohibits commercial use/planting of GE crops; trials confined to lab greenhouses. Real R&D capacity (biotech cotton/potato lines in lab) but commercialisation blocked pending legal reform. EAEU member, not EU.

countries.name: Kyrgyzstan
countries.ge_status: Law banning cultivation, production, import and sale of GMO-containing products; as an EAEU member must tolerate up to 0.9% content. New Law on Biological Safety is control-oriented. Strongly anti-GMO politically.

countries.name: Moldova
countries.ge_status: No commercial GM cultivation; gene-edited plants classified as GMOs (2022) - importable but not cultivable, mirroring the EU. Active EU accession candidate on an accelerated track - will transpose the EU NGT regulation, the key driver for earlier adoption.

countries.name: North Macedonia
countries.ge_status: 2013 ban on production/marketing of GMO foods explicitly framed '...until it becomes an EU member'; import of GMO food not allowed. EU candidate (negotiations opened 2022) - its own law signals it will lift the ban and adopt EU (now NGT) rules on accession.

countries.name: Serbia
countries.ge_status: Law on GMOs (2009) bans all commercial cultivation AND trade of GMOs - one of Europe's strictest regimes. 150+ municipalities signed an anti-GMO declaration. EU candidate, but the GMO law is itself the blocker stalling accession Chapter 30; strong political resistance. Eventual EU-driven change like

countries.name: Tajikistan
countries.ge_status: No commercial GM cultivation; no detailed/active modern biotech framework. Cartagena Protocol party but minimal implementation. Undeveloped/de facto restrictive; very limited capacity.

countries.name: Turkmenistan
countries.ge_status: No GM cultivation; restrictive approach to GMO-containing products; one of the least developed/most closed biotech environments in the region.

countries.name: Ukraine
countries.ge_status: No GE events currently approved. New Law #3339-IX (adopted 2023, replacing the old Biosafety Law from Sept 2026) creates EU-style GMO registration/labelling built on EU acts per the EU-Ukraine Association Agreement. Gene editing not yet specifically regulated, but an active EU accession candidate (n

countries.name: Uzbekistan
countries.ge_status: No commercial GM cultivation; no dedicated biosafety law. Presidential Decree PQ-4899 (2020) promotes genetic engineering, conflicting with a 2022 organic-products GMO prohibition. The most developmentally inclined Central Asian state but lacks enabling legislation. No EU/EAEU accession driver.
